  • Can losing your sense of smell or taste mean COVID-19?
Family Health

Can losing your sense of smell or taste mean COVID-19?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A sudden change in smell or taste can be a symptom of COVID-19, including when your nose does not feel blocked. It is a clue to consider alongside testing and the rest of your health, rather than a diagnosis on its own. Understanding what has changed can help you seek the right care and manage everyday life during recovery.

A new change can be an early clue

COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, a virus that can produce a wide range of symptoms. Some people first notice that a familiar drink has little aroma, or that food seems strangely flavourless. The change may appear before, alongside or after other symptoms. It can happen without a blocked nose, but it does not happen to everyone who has the infection.

Colds, flu and sinus inflammation can also temporarily interfere with smell. A new change therefore deserves attention without being treated as a diagnosis. Note when it started, whether it was sudden or gradual, and whether there is congestion, fever or another illness. Being able to smell normally does not rule COVID-19 out.

Smell, taste and flavour are related but different

Your tongue and other taste-sensitive areas recognise qualities such as sweetness, saltiness, sourness, bitterness and savouriness. Smell adds much of the detail that distinguishes one food from another. Aromas reach the nose both when you sniff and from the back of the mouth while eating. That is why a stuffy nose can make a meal seem dull.

A person may still detect that chocolate is sweet while missing its familiar flavour. However, not every taste complaint is simply a smell problem: true changes in taste can occur too. There is no useful rule that a fixed percentage of everyone’s taste loss must come from smell. Describing the two experiences separately helps a clinician assess them.

Loss, reduction and distortion can all occur

Anosmia means loss of smell; hyposmia means a reduced ability to smell. With parosmia, something familiar smells different, often unpleasant. Phantosmia describes an odour perceived when there is no source. Taste may similarly be reduced, absent or altered, including an unwanted metallic or bitter sensation.

These descriptions identify an experience, not its cause. Someone who starts noticing distorted smells during recovery has not necessarily caught COVID-19 again. Conversely, a fresh respiratory illness should not automatically be dismissed as part of an older smell problem. Tell the clinician which changes are new and which have continued since the original illness.

What researchers learned about the nose

Smell receptors work within a specialised lining high in the nose. The virus uses entry machinery that includes a receptor called ACE2. Early research examined where the relevant genes and proteins were present, to understand why smell could disappear even without the congestion typical of a cold.

A 2020 study identified viral-entry-related molecules particularly in non-neuronal supporting cells rather than the smell-sensing neurons themselves. Disruption of those supporting tissues offered a plausible explanation for altered smell. This was evidence about a mechanism, not proof that every patient has the same injury or that a home symptom can reveal which cells are affected. The biology of persistent symptoms is more complex than a single receptor explanation.

Why older percentages need context

An early review combined twenty-four studies involving 8,438 people with confirmed COVID-19. Its pooled estimates were about 41% for smell disturbance and 38% for taste disturbance. Individual studies differed enormously, reflecting their populations, timing and ways of asking about or measuring symptoms. Those findings describe the early pandemic, not the proportion expected in every outbreak today.

That review found lower reported prevalence in studies with an older average age and higher detection when smell was measured rather than only self-reported. It did not find a significant overall difference by sex, although individual studies reported different patterns. None of these observations allows a person to decide whether they have COVID-19 based on age or sex. Circulating variants, immunity and study methods also matter.

Smell loss does not predict a mild course

Some early observational reports found smell changes more often among people treated outside hospital than among those with severe illness. Such an association does not establish that smell loss protects someone, or that a person who loses smell cannot become seriously unwell. The groups being compared may differ in several other ways.

Assess the whole illness. Breathing, alertness, chest symptoms, hydration and relevant medical conditions matter more than whether coffee has an aroma. Do not delay medical help because a symptom list or an old study has described this particular sign as reassuring.

Notice everyday changes without unsafe self-testing

It can help to explain that you no longer recognise the usual aroma of prepared coffee, garlic in a meal or another familiar food. You may also notice whether a small amount of an ordinary food still seems sweet, salty, sour or bitter. Use only foods you normally tolerate; there is no need to eat something that conflicts with an allergy or dietary restriction.

This is an observation for your history, not a COVID-19 test. Do not inhale baby powder or loose spices, put substances inside your nose, sniff solvents or cleaning products, or use a flame to test smell. Strong irritation is a different sensation and does not prove that the smell system is working. Formal smell and taste testing uses controlled methods.

Use appropriate infection testing

For a new unexplained change, follow local guidance on COVID-19 testing. A rapid antigen test can be negative early in infection. FDA advice for someone with symptoms is to repeat a negative home antigen test after 48 hours, giving at least two tests over three days. Follow the particular kit’s instructions; a clinician may recommend a molecular test.

If you have symptoms and a negative result, continue precautions while the cause is uncertain. A negative test does not explain persistent smell loss or exclude another respiratory illness. High-risk people should contact a clinician promptly rather than waiting to complete repeated tests before asking about treatment.

Look for the rest of the symptom picture

COVID-19 may also cause fever or chills, cough, tiredness, sore throat, a runny or blocked nose, headache, body aches or breathlessness. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea can occur. Symptoms can change as the illness develops, and some people have only a few of them.

Flu and other infections can look similar. Neither this list nor a smell change reliably distinguishes one virus from another. When contacting a healthcare service, give the symptom start date, test results and any change in breathing or ability to drink. Mention pregnancy, relevant conditions and medicines because they can affect the next steps.

Ask early about treatment when risk is higher

Older age, a weakened immune system and conditions such as chronic lung or heart disease can increase the chance of severe illness. Diabetes, obesity and pregnancy or recent pregnancy may also be relevant to an individual assessment. A clinician can consider the combination of factors rather than relying on one symptom.

Some antiviral options must start within five days of the first symptoms, and another commonly used option within seven. Ask promptly even if the illness seems mild. The prescriber checks suitability and medicine interactions. Treatment for the infection does not guarantee recovery of smell, and an altered taste can sometimes be a medicine side effect.

Reduce spread while you are unwell

Stay home and reduce close contact when you have a new respiratory illness that is not better explained by another cause. Cleaner indoor air and a well-fitting mask can help when sharing space, particularly with someone at higher risk. The advice that applies depends on where you live and the setting.

For general community settings, CDC guidance uses two conditions that have both been met for at least 24 hours: symptoms are improving overall, and there has been no fever without fever-reducing medicine. It then advises five days of extra precautions. If fever returns or you worsen, stay home again. Healthcare and other specific settings have separate rules; persistent smell loss alone cannot measure contagiousness.

Know when help is urgent

Get emergency help for difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, or inability to wake or stay awake. Depending on skin tone, lips, nail beds or skin may look unusually pale, grey or blue. Do not wait for a positive test or a change in smell before responding.

Seek advice sooner for other severe or worrying symptoms, deterioration or difficulty maintaining fluids. A smell change following a significant head injury also needs assessment in that context. If weakness, trouble speaking or another sudden neurological symptom occurs, treat it as an emergency rather than assuming a respiratory infection.

Recovery studies do not set a deadline

In an early CDC outpatient study, smell and taste symptoms that had resolved by the follow-up interview had a median resolution time of eight days from the test date. That calculation concerned people whose symptom had ended; it did not mean every participant recovered within eight days. It also was not a promise measured from the first day of illness.

A small European report from 2020 described an average smell-loss duration of 8.9 days and recovery within twenty-eight days in 98% of its affected patients. Its size, retrospective reporting and early-pandemic setting limit how broadly that figure can be applied. Some people recover over weeks or months, while others have longer-lasting or incomplete recovery. A cold-related change also has no universal three-to-seven-day deadline.

Other causes deserve consideration

Nasal allergies, sinus infection and polyps can reduce the arrival of odours at the smell-sensitive area. Smoking, head injury, dental problems and exposure to irritant chemicals or solvents can also be relevant. Mention recent nose, mouth or throat surgery, including sinus or dental procedures, and any head-and-neck radiotherapy.

Medicines can contribute, including some antibiotics, antihistamines and blood-pressure treatments. Do not stop prescribed treatment on your own; a pharmacist or prescriber can review the timing and alternatives. Taste changes may relate to oral health as well as to the nose, so an examination may need to consider both.

Less common conditions are assessed in context

Hormonal and neurological conditions are among the less common explanations. Thyroid problems and conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease or multiple sclerosis may affect smell. A small study also found smell and taste impairment in people with Cushing’s syndrome. These associations do not make smell loss a screening test for any of those conditions.

Rarely, a growth or another structural problem may need investigation. The clinician uses the pattern, examination and accompanying symptoms to decide what is appropriate. A long list of possible causes does not mean that everyone needs a brain scan or an extensive hormone panel. Persistent or progressive symptoms should be assessed rather than assigned to a past infection indefinitely.

Get support for persistent changes

Arrange a medical review if smell has not returned to normal within a few weeks, or earlier if there are concerning symptoms or trouble eating and drinking. Assessment may include the nose and mouth, medical history, a medicine review and supervised smell or taste tests. Treating an identified sinus or nasal condition may help.

Smell training helps some people, although benefit and speed of recovery vary. Ask a clinician or established smell-disorder service for an appropriate method. Do not start steroid treatment, high-dose supplements or concentrated products in the nose without advice. If distorted flavours are limiting meals, a dietitian can help you maintain nutrition; changes in food temperature or texture may be easier to tolerate.

Make daily life safer while you recover

Check smoke alarms and appropriate gas-safety arrangements rather than trusting your nose to detect a problem. Carbon monoxide has no smell even for someone with normal senses, so a suitable alarm matters independently of smell loss. Follow food-storage instructions and use-by dates; tasting questionable food is not a safe substitute for smelling it.

Loss of enjoyment in food, anxiety about safety and feeling disconnected from familiar smells can affect mood and relationships. Explain what has changed to people who support you. Ask for help with poor intake, weight loss or distress. Recovery can be uncertain without making those practical and emotional needs any less important.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Smell and taste changes have several causes. Current infection guidance and an individual assessment should guide testing, precautions and treatment.

Historical studies explain what was observed early in the pandemic; they do not predict current prevalence, illness severity or a personal recovery date.

How BeMama can help

Write down when the change began, what you can still detect and any new symptoms. Bring that short record and your medicine list to an appointment.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for breathing difficulty, persistent chest pressure, new confusion or inability to stay awake. Higher-risk people should ask promptly about time-sensitive treatment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A new smell or taste change can occur with COVID-19, but normal smell does not exclude infection.
  • Smell-related flavour changes and true taste changes are not identical.
  • Early-pandemic percentages and short recovery averages are not personal guarantees.
  • Use appropriate tests and timely care; do not rely on unsafe kitchen experiments.
  • Persistent symptoms deserve assessment, nutrition support and practical home-safety adjustments.

Frequently asked questions

Can smell loss happen before a cough or fever?

Yes. It may precede, accompany or follow other symptoms, and sometimes occurs without nasal blockage. Its timing alone does not confirm COVID-19.

Does being able to smell exclude COVID-19?

No. Many infections occur without smell loss. Testing and the overall clinical picture are more informative.

Is bland food always a taste disorder?

No. Smell supplies much of flavour, so food can seem bland while basic tastes remain detectable. True taste changes are also possible and deserve separate description.

Can I test myself with coffee or cinnamon?

Noticing a familiar food’s aroma can help describe the change, but it cannot diagnose infection. Do not inhale powders, irritants or chemicals; use an appropriate COVID-19 test.

What if my first rapid test is negative?

It may be too early to detect infection. Follow the kit and local guidance; FDA advice for symptomatic people includes another antigen test after 48 hours. Ask promptly about care if you are at higher risk.

Does losing smell mean my illness will stay mild?

No. It is not protection against severe illness. Seek help according to breathing, chest symptoms, alertness and other warning signs.

Should smell return within eight days?

There is no such deadline. The early eight-day estimate applied to resolved symptoms in a particular study. Recovery can take weeks or months and may be incomplete.

Why do familiar foods suddenly smell unpleasant?

This can be parosmia, a distortion of smell that sometimes occurs after infection. Seek support if it affects intake or persists; it does not by itself prove reinfection.

Should I stop medicine that might affect taste?

No. Ask the prescriber or pharmacist to review it. Stopping treatment without a plan may create a different health problem.

When should persistent smell loss be reviewed?

Arrange assessment if it has not returned to normal within a few weeks, or sooner for progressive symptoms, an injury, difficulty eating or drinking, or other concerns. Emergency symptoms need immediate help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
